title: Content to seem foolish
hook: if you want to improve, be willing to look foolish about outside things (Enchiridion 13)

segments.voice: Yesterday: ataraxia, the price of calm. Your line was nothing is had for nothing. When a small loss came, did you pay the price and move on? Day three hundred forty-five.

Athens. A merchant named Zeno, recently shipwrecked, has found a teacher: Crates the Cynic. The story comes from Diogenes Laertius. One day Crates hands him a pot of lentil soup and tells him to carry it through the busy potters' quarter. Zeno tries to hide the pot under his cloak, embarrassed. Crates cracks it with his staff, and soup runs down Zeno's legs. Zeno bolts. Crates calls after him, roughly: why run away, little Phoenician? Nothing terrible has happened to you. Zeno would go on to found the Stoic school. Today: content to seem foolish.
screen: `ZENO AND A POT OF SOUP.` → `CRATES CRACKS IT.` → `NOTHING TERRIBLE HAS HAPPENED.`

segments.voice: First, the instruction. Section thirteen of the handbook says: if you want to make progress, be content to be thought foolish and simple about outside things. Not foolish about everything. About the outside things: the latest phone, the right restaurant, the gossip, who's up and who's down. Second, the harder half. Don't wish to be thought to know anything, Epictetus says. And if people start to think you're somebody, be suspicious of yourself. That's a striking line from a famous teacher. It sounds like Socrates in Plato's Apology, who says he is wiser only in not thinking he knows what he doesn't. Third, the reason. It isn't easy, he says, to keep your purpose in line with nature and also keep up with all the outside things. Care for one, and you're bound to neglect the other. Attention is limited. Spend it on looking clever and there's less left for being good. Fourth, why it's training. Looking foolish can feel like a small death. The red face, the wish to explain. That's exactly what Crates' soup pot was training. Each time you survive it, you learn the thing Crates shouted: nothing terrible has happened. You asked the obvious question in the meeting, and the meeting went on. You wore last year's coat, and the sun came up. You said I don't know, and someone finally explained it. People may think you're a little behind. Let them think it. Meanwhile, your attention is free for what's really yours.
screen: `FOOLISH ABOUT OUTSIDE THINGS.` · `DON'T WISH TO SEEM TO KNOW.` · `ATTENTION IS LIMITED.` · `NOTHING TERRIBLE HAS HAPPENED.` · then, large: `LET THEM THINK IT.`

segments.voice: Think of one place today where you usually perform knowing. A meeting, a class, a conversation about something you're supposed to understand. Picture yourself there, asking the simple question, or saying, I don't actually know what that means. Feel the flush of it. Let it rise and pass. Then hear Crates' line, gently this time: nothing terrible has happened. Decide where you'll try it for real. The bell holds the time.
Crates, the Cynic who cracked Zeno's soup pot to teach him this: let people think you simple about outside things, and keep your attention for what's yours. Today's word.
Your line: let them think it. Look foolish once today, on purpose and kindly: ask the obvious question, or admit you don't know. Day three hundred forty-five.

howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners deliberately accept looking uninformed or unfashionable about outside matters, as training in caring less about others' opinions.

fork.setup: you're Zeno. soup is running down your legs in the potters' quarter. what do you do?
fork.reveal: Zeno ran. Crates called after him: nothing terrible has happened to you. the lesson stuck; Zeno founded the Stoic school.

trapdoor: what you thought: don't care what anyone thinks.
what it means: be willing to look simple about outside things, so your attention stays on what's yours.
what a scholar hears: Zeno's soup-pot lesson from Crates (Diogenes Laertius 7.3) puts a Cynic lesson at the start of the Stoic story.

sources.work: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers

notes: Review (2026-10-01): cut the unsourced date 'around three hundred BC' and 'young' (Diogenes Laertius gives his age as thirty); removed 'the man Epictetus admired most' and made the Socrates line match Apology 21d (cited); 'likely neglect' corrected to the text's necessity; 'to a lot of us' and 'the Stoics practiced it' softened; named Diogenes Laertius in the voice so the myth item is answerable.

Zeno, Crates and the lentil soup in the Kerameikos (potters' quarter): Diogenes Laertius 7.3; Zeno's shipwreck 7.2. Date 'around three hundred BC' is approximate. Confirm details and the quoted rebuke (paraphrased, no quotation marks).
Greek ἠλίθιος in Enchiridion 13 ('ἀνόητος καὶ ἠλίθιος'): confirm.
Socrates as the figure Epictetus most admired: standard; confirm phrasing.
